demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Mary, a 47-year-old African American architect married for over two decades, has been struggling with the aftermath of an accident that occurred several months ago. While at work on a construction site, she accidentally caused serious injury to one of her colleagues, leaving him hospitalized and partially disabled. Since then, Mary's life has been marked by a profound sense of guilt and an overwhelming need to prevent such an incident from happening again. Mary had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, which deepened her feelings of isolation and set apartness from others. This self-comparison often led her to dwell on what she perceived as her own inadequacies, perpetuating a cycle of self-blame rumination. Her belief in herself as an unrecognizable person further intensified these negative appraisals, leading her to perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again. The difficulty Mary experienced when trying to deliberately recall the accident made it hard for her to process what had happened. When she did remember, the vividness of sensory details—like the taste she could still experience and the sounds that echoed in her mind—only exacerbated her distress. These memories often triggered false alarms, making her react as if she were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. Mary's intense focus on preventing a recurrence through these rituals led to further difficulty concentrating, which had concrete consequences at work. Her attentional lapses and frequent startle responses to ordinary sounds made it challenging for her to maintain her professional performance, leading to some minor mistakes that she felt unable to overlook given the gravity of her accident. The memory of the accident also fueled Mary's sense of isolation, as she found herself increasingly withdrawing from social interactions. She believed no one else could truly understand what she was going through, which further reinforced her negative appraisals and made her even more prone to self-blame rumination. This cycle intensified her false alarms, making her jump at every sound or unexpected noise. As the weeks passed, Mary's mental rituals became more elaborate, consuming significant portions of her day. She found herself performing these routines compulsively, hoping they would keep her safe and prevent another accident. However, this preoccupation further hindered her ability to concentrate and engage with her surroundings, deepening her sense of isolation. Mary’s husband noticed the changes in his wife's behavior but couldn't fully understand what was driving them. Her constant mental rituals and avoidance behaviors strained their relationship, as she found it increasingly difficult to connect emotionally with him or anyone else. The memory of the accident remained vivid and intrusive, and her attempts to control these thoughts only seemed to make them more persistent. Finally, Mary realized that her life had become unmanageable. She was afraid that if she didn't seek help, her work performance would continue to decline, further isolating her from both her professional and personal life. What frightened her most was the possibility of another accident and the feeling that she could never truly be the person she once was. Mary came to therapy hoping for a way out of this relentless cycle. She was seeking tools to manage her memories and fears so she could regain control over her life and reconnect with those around her.
